each question in your head or on paper first, then open the answer under it.

Every term is defined on the slides: [Week 11, Wrangling the Data](../decks/mc501/w11-wrangling.html).
The full explanation is in [Chapter 11](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v/chapters/chapter11.html).

## 1. What data wrangling is

Which of these is **data wrangling**?

- **A.** Reading thirty chat messages and coding each one as a reaction or as commentary
- **B.** Adding a `message_length` column that counts the characters in each message
- **C.** Writing the hypothesis for the study
- **D.** Choosing which journal to submit the study to

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 1</summary>

**B.** **Data wrangling** is getting data into a form you can analyze: tidying it (one row per
case, one column per variable) and transforming it (keeping rows, adding columns, summarizing,
joining tables). Adding a column computed from the data is a transformation. A is hand-coding,
which records a value by a written rule. C and D are part of designing and publishing the study.

</details>

## 2. Tidy data

A table of Reddit comments has a `tags` column, and one of its cells reads `politics, satire`.
Which tidy-data rule does that cell break, and how would you fix it?

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 2</summary>

**One value per cell.** Tidy data has one observation per row, one variable per column, and one
value per cell. Two tags in one cell hide two values in one place, so R cannot count or filter
them cleanly. One fix is a row per comment and tag; another is one yes-or-no column per tag. Which
fits depends on what one row of your data is meant to be.

</details>

## 3. Reading a pipe

Read this code aloud, then say what it does, step by step.

```r
chat %>%
  filter(channel == "bobross") %>%
  select(sender, message)
```

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 3</summary>

Read **`%>%`** as "and then." Take the chat table, **and then** keep only the rows from Bob
Ross's channel, **and then** keep only the `sender` and `message` columns. The **pipe** hands the
result of one line to the next, so the code reads in the same order the steps happen.

</details>

## 4. The timestamp

The first message's `date` reads `1542578127023`. If you hand that number straight to
`as_datetime()`, every message is dated around the year 50,850. Why, and what does
`as_datetime(date / 1000)` do about it?

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 4</summary>

A **timestamp** is the date and time something happened. This one counts **milliseconds** since
midnight on 1 January 1970 (the Unix epoch), and `as_datetime()` expects **seconds**, so it reads
a number a thousand times too large. `date / 1000` turns milliseconds into seconds first, and
then `as_datetime()` turns the seconds into a date and time.

</details>

## 5. A rolling join

Chat messages arrive every second; stream snapshots come every few minutes. Why can the two
tables not be joined on an exact time, and what does the rolling join match instead?

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 5</summary>

Almost no message shares its exact time with a snapshot, so an exact match would leave nearly
every message unmatched. A **join** puts two tables together by matching a shared key, and a
**rolling join** lets the time part of that key match the nearest earlier value: the same
channel, and the latest snapshot at or before the message. In dplyr that is
`join_by(channel, closest(ts >= snapshot_ts))`, after a `select()` that renames the snapshot's
time to `snapshot_ts`.

</details>

## 6. When the keys do not match

One table writes the channel as `#bobross`, the other as `bobross`. You join them by `channel`.
What do the joined columns hold, and will R give you an error?

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 6</summary>

The joined columns are all `NA`, and **R gives no error**. The **key** is the column two tables
share, which says which row in one goes with which row in the other. `#bobross` and `bobross` are
different values to R, so no row finds a match. Check the key column in both tables before every
join, and count the new column afterward.

</details>

## 7. More rows after a join

`chat_streams` has 35,267 rows. After `left_join(channel_type, by = "channel")`, the result has
more. What does that tell you about `channel_type`?

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 7</summary>

**`channel_type` has duplicate keys:** at least one channel appears in it more than once.
`left_join()` keeps every row of the left table and gives it one copy for each matching row on
the right, so a channel listed twice doubles each of its messages. A lookup table needs one row
per key, which is why Step 2 keeps one category per channel.

</details>

## 8. The 501 unlabeled messages

After the join, `count(is_gaming)` shows `TRUE`, `FALSE`, and 501 rows of `NA`. Those messages
come from the two channels with no category ever recorded. What should happen to them, and where
does that decision belong?

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 8</summary>

**Leave them as `NA`, and say so in a comment.** A **missing value** is a cell with nothing in it,
which R prints as `NA`. The data does not say whether those two channels are gaming channels, so
`NA` is the correct outcome, and their 501 messages are left out of the gaming comparison. How you
handle missing values is a methodological decision, so it belongs in the script, commented, where
a reviewer can find it.

</details>
